title: Architecture surgery: Mistral/Llama/Qwen MoE routing & KV prewarm review
transcript:
Meeting header: Feb 11 2026 15:30 UTC — Duration ~72m
Attendees (as logged): Alex Kim, Samira Patel, Diego Vargas, Jia Wang — Daniel Wu, Maya Lopez, Owen Reid, Priyanka Rao, Tom Becker
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/decks/mistral-qwen-tuning-v1.pdf ; internal benchmark sheet (shared in chat)

[00:00] Alex Kim: Okay hi everyone, thanks for making time, we'll jump in — this is the architecture surgery session we've called to look at the latency tail and cost tradeoffs across your mixed model fleet.
[00:18] Daniel Wu: Hi, yeah thanks. We had some ticket spikes last week after rollout; tail latency for Qwen in VPC jumped. Looking for root cause and whether KV prewarm or different routing helps.
[00:30] Samira Patel: Great — quick agenda: 1) recap your current topology and SLA targets, 2) examine KV cache hit patterns and cold-starts, 3) routing thresholds for MoE, 4) rope scaling/position-embedding effects across Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen, 5) concrete tuning steps + pilot plan.
[01:05] Maya Lopez: Quick context — production is a private VPC on our colo racks, dedicated nodes for Llama-70b-ish and Mistral 23B, and a Qwen-34b MoE variant on a separate pool. We use token-affinity routing and a small prefix cache.
[01:30] Jia Wang: Can you share the SLOs?
[01:34] Tom Becker: 95th < 180ms for chat, p95 generation; p99 we try to keep under 800ms but that's slipping.
[01:45] Samira: Good. So first, KV cache — our traces show a hit rate of around 54% for chat flows and heavy variability during bursts. When hit-rate drops, microbatches shrink, throughput drops and latency spikes.
[02:20] Daniel: That matches what we see. We also noticed that when Qwen gets routing load, other models degrade: CPU/mem behind autoscaler spikes.
[02:35] Diego Vargas: Two quick hypotheses: 1) router thresholds are too permissive and are sending low-affinity tokens to MoE experts causing cross-socket KV fetches; 2) ROPE/positional decay mismatch between models causing cache fragmentation.
[03:00] Owen Reid: Cache fragmentation? explain?
[03:03] Samira: Sure — if you have prefix caching keyed by full KV context plus position bucket, and your rope scaling (frequency of positional embeddings) differs between model families (e.g., Llama uses one decay curve, Qwen different), then the same user prompt token sequences map to different cache keys when model variant changes. That reduces effective reuse.
[03:40] Priyanka Rao: On security side, note we need KMS integration for on-prem keys and audit logs — any route changes must preserve the customer key flow.
[03:50] Alex: Noted. We'll not change key handling.
[03:56] Samira: Back to routing: for MoE we recommend adaptive thresholding — set gating softmax top-2 but with a per-token confidence threshold. If gating confidence < 0.6, route to a smaller dense fallback model to avoid expensive expert dispatches.
[04:25] Daniel: We feared that — won't fallback harm quality?
[04:30] Jia: We tested with tuned prompts; quality hit was ~2.5 BLEU-equivalent-ish on our eval set but latency/cost improved 20–35% during bursts. It's a tradeoff: can set canary on a subset of traffic.
[04:52] Tom: Is there a way to estimate cost delta before rollout?
[04:55] Diego: Yes — we have the per-token kernel-time profile and a simulator we can run against your traffic trace. We ran a sim with your last two weeks and predicted MoE routing reduction from 42% to 26% of tokens hitting experts -> estimated 28% cost drop. We'll share the sim CSV.
[05:25] Alex: Let's dig into prewarm and KV. How many warmup tokens do you retain?
[05:30] Maya: We keep a 4k prefix cache keyed per user session, TTL 10 minutes.
[05:35] Jia: For mixed models that's thin. We recommend a small LRU per-socket prewarm that stores just the KV for the last N prefixes with normalized rope positions — i.e., remap positions into canonical buckets so variants with similar rope scaling can reuse.
[06:05] Daniel: Normalized rope positions — can you be concrete?
[06:10] Samira: Yes — implement a translation layer at routing time: when tokenizing you produce a canonical positional index (e.g., scaled to 512 buckets) and store KV cache with that canonical index. At model selection time, translate canonical -> model rope scale. It won't be perfect but will recover a chunk of hits that otherwise miss.
[06:35] Owen: Sounds complex for on-prem? Requires changes in runtime?
[06:38] Jia: Minimal — the router layer already touches token metadata; we add a deterministic mapping function and store secondary index. No model weights change. On prewarm we also suggest prefix compaction to reduce KV size.
[06:55] Daniel: Any gotchas on quantization interaction? we run 8-bit QAT for Llama but Qwen we've been conservative.
[07:05] Diego: Quantization affects numeric fidelity of KV values; for KV cache reuse across quant modes, we recommend storing a higher-fidelity prewarm snapshot (float16) in shared NVM and convert on the hot path. That avoids cross-quant mismatch and reduces cold penalty.
[07:30] Priyanka: But storing float16 persistent snapshots has compliance implications — are keys encrypted?
[07:35] Alex: Yes KMS encrypt at rest in your VPC — we'll include encryption patterns in the security pack.
[07:44] Priyanka: okay thanks.
[07:48] [08:00] Samira: Let's talk rope scaling specifics: Llama models we saw are robust to linear rope decay scaling up to 1.3x without quality loss for chat, Mistral is more sensitive; Qwen's positional embeddings interact with MoE gating and can amplify decay effects.
[08:22] Maya: We observed hallucination spikes when we scaled rope down on Mistral.
[08:25] Jia: Right — Mistral's attention heads have tighter positional coupling. We recommend per-model rope multipliers: Llama 1.2, Mistral 0.95, Qwen 1.05 as starting point in your mixed fleet.
[08:45] Daniel: Are those applied at compile time? runtime?
[08:49] Samira: Runtime hyperparam remap layer in the runtime kernel selection path; it's a cheap multiplier applied before attention score calc — you can toggle via model variant flags.
[09:05] Tom: Ok but we need to test for regression.
[09:08] Alex: We'll ship an eval harness that runs your golden prompts against each rope setting and returns per-example delta. We'll also add a drift alarm.
[09:20] [09:30] Diego: Batching and microbatching: your microbatch size collapses when KV miss rate grows, which triggers more forwarding calls and increases p99. Two levers: increase prewarm concurrency or allow slightly larger batching delays (add 3–6ms tail latency) to improve token amortization.
[09:50] Tom: Can't increase delay - chat is interactive.
[09:52] Jia: Then prewarm is the better path — proactively warm KV for sessions predicted to have high fanout. Use a lightweight predictor on your gateway - if user session shows > 6 turns in 10s we prewarm. We can share a small ML predictor.
[10:15] Daniel: What about autoscaler settings? We see spikes in CPU while GPUs wait.
[10:20] Owen: GPU cold starts are expensive in on-prem.
[10:24] Samira: Tune allocators to keep a minimal pool of warm GPU contexts and use fast VM reuse. For on-prem, dedicated node pools with lower eviction gives better tail latency at cost of steady-state spend.
[10:40] Priyanka: Are there recommendations for network topology? we use SR-IOV.
[10:44] Diego: Keep the model-serving fabric isolated, use jumbo frames and ensure NIC queues map to hardware contexts; if you have cross-socket KV fetches, that adds 4–12ms.
[10:58] [11:10] Daniel: Let's look at the demo benchmarks you shared in chat — the sim that predicts 28% saving.
[11:15] Alex: Right, we ran 3 sims: A baseline, B with adaptive MoE thresholds and fallback, C with adaptive plus canonical-KV prewarm and rope remap. Results: B -> 28% cost, C -> 42% cost drop and p99 improved 18%.
[11:35] Maya: C looks good but more complex. How long to pilot?
[11:40] Samira: We estimate 3 weeks: week 1 config-only canary, week 2 run sim-based warmup and observe, week 3 expand to 50% traffic.
[11:52] Jia: We'll instrument additional metrics: expert dispatch rate, per-token gating confidence histogram, canonical-KV hit-rate, rope-translation delta.
[12:05] [12:20] Tom: Security checklist?
[12:22] Alex: We'll send security pack: SOC2 artifacts, KMS diagram, network segmentation guide, SSO/SAML flow, RBAC matrix.
[12:30] Priyanka: We need to review HSM/KMS compatibility with our HSM vendor.
[12:34] Diego: We'll coordinate with your infra.
[12:36] [12:40] Daniel: A couple of nitty details — we run mixed-precision kernels; will rope remap affect kernel selection?
[12:44] Jia: Kernel selection uses sequence length, batch shape, and rope multiplier. Small changes are supported; we will run precompile step for hot variants.
[12:55] Alex: Any competitors in play?
[12:58] Daniel: We are also trialing FastServe and CloudModelX for comparison.
[13:03] Diego: Noted. Our sim includes a multi-model baseline so you can compare.
[13:12] [13:20] Action recap and next steps — let's capture next steps now.
[13:24] Alex: Recap: 1) We'll share the detailed sim CSV and the bench harness, 2) Redwood to provide a config patch for adaptive MoE threshold + fallback, 3) provide canonical-KV prewarm design doc and a small prototype to run in your VPC, 4) security pack with KMS/HSM notes, 5) schedule pilot kickoff on Feb 23.
[13:46] Daniel: Feb 23 works. We'll also run a local trace export and send it by Feb 16.
[13:54] Priyanka: Please include encryption-at-rest details for float16 snapshots.
[13:58] Alex: Will do.
[14:00] Samira: Anything else?
[14:05] Maya: Could we try a quick smoke: enable adaptive threshold on 5% traffic for next 48 hours?
[14:09] Alex: Yes we can do that as a first micro-canary.
[14:12] Tom: Please also add a cost projection with dedicated pool vs burst to hosted fallback.
[14:16] Alex: We'll add that.
[14:20] Daniel: Thanks everyone. Great session.
[14:22] Alex: End notes — we'll follow up with the deck and action items in CRM.
summary: Redwood and NeuroScale reviewed on-prem deployment issues: high p99 and cost driven by KV miss rates and MoE expert dispatches. Recommendations: adaptive MoE gating with dense fallback, canonicalized rope-position mapping to improve KV reuse across model families, KV prewarm snapshots in float16 with KMS encryption, and tuned autoscaler and prewarm heuristics. Agreed pilot plan: 3-week rollout starting Feb 23 with canary, sim data to be shared by Redwood and trace by NeuroScale.
next_steps: Redwood: share sim CSV and bench harness (by 2026-02-13)
NeuroScale: export and send full trace (by 2026-02-16)
Redwood: provide config patch for adaptive MoE thresholds (by 2026-02-17)
action_items: Alex Kim — send security pack + KMS/HSM notes (due 2026-02-13)
Samira Patel — supply sim CSV and recommended thresholds (due 2026-02-13)
Daniel Wu — export trace & provide topology docs (due 2026-02-16)
